posts.author: ElvenNeko
posts.body:
Hi. I need some advice about publishing my next game.
I am a writer and a bit of game designer. Not long ago I came close to finishing my 4-th game. I work alone on it, so I don’t respond to anyone and can make whatever choices I want about it (I clarify that in case of anyone asking about what other members of the team want).
My previous 3 games were free. There were several reasons for that, but the main one is that I always wanted for anyone to be able to play my game. Living in Ukraine, where economical situation ever changed only for the worse, I could not afford to buy many games, so I had to resort to piracy, and I still do, because some games now can cost more than my entire month income. Experiencing interactive stories helped me to survive in society that has no place for disabled people, and I want to do the same for others who are in need of something positive in the lives. So my next game will be free as well.
But, at the same time I consider making a paid version in Steam. Why?
Pros:
- My debts are increasing, my cats getting sick and it eats away all my money. And the prices on everything rise as UAH course keeps worsening, and government is planning to increase communal service prices a lot without ever increasing incomes. So any extra cash will be helpful to pay either debts or medicine.
- I don’t understand marketing, at all. Max I can do is throw a couple of posts on reddit gaming subs. Steam will automatically give some visibility for the game. From all my previous games most popular were the one I released on Steam.  People will still be able to torrent the game, try it out and buy it after if they like it.
- In current state of my country and my health this is probably my last game, so I just curious to see how commercial release would work out
- Steam has forums where people could discuss the game, and reviews where they can write feedback
Cons:
- Entry fee. It’s the biggest issue for me, because it’s almost my entire income for 2 months. Will I be able to return this money? If yes, then it’s nothing to worry about. If no, my debt will increase.
- Availability. Steam removed the standard methods to replenish it’s purse from my country, idk why. There are other methods described online, but not sure if they still work.
- Niche. Being a solo dev without any art or programmer knowledge is very limiting. So I had to cut out a lot of ideas, including combat, turning the game into hybrid between the quest and visual novel. Think of Dreamfall series, but with less puzzles and more dialogue. This genre has fans, but is not so much as some of the others. It's also not super impressive visually – I can’t draw, and all of my budget for this game went on chocolate and antidepressants. I does not mean I did not try to make it look pretty and have nice details – once I spent entire day on making an elevator opening animation, and did a lot of other small, but cool details. Also my friend helped me to fix some of the most problematic visual issues, so now it’s not bad either. Just a bit minimalistic in some places.
And if that wasn’t enough, in this game I decided to try out things I never tried before, starting for the genre – parody.  I am usually quite certain in quality of my plots because I understand the art of storytelling well, but that is only true because I have lots of experience in genres I work with. Parody is not one of them – it’s a rare genre, and a complicated one, because you need to balance references and general humor very carefully, to avoid situations where people without extra knowledge will not see anything funny at all. Also my sense of humor were always quite weird: I rarely found mainstream comedies funny, and preferred the absurd type of humor, like movies with Leslie Nilsen. Also, like South Park show or games i decided to parody some of the social issues. So I had a lot of ideas for jokes in this game, but not sure how funny they will be to the others. Also, the game is part musical. And musical is also a niche genre.
So I ended up having a triple-n game – quest, parody, musical (I wonder if I should put it in the description?). I believe that with proper marketing it could find the playerbase, but with it being limited to standard amount of Steam views I have doubts that it will be large enough to at least pay back the entry fee (I don’t plan to put a high price on it since it’s quite short). I showed parts of the game to my friends, one of them even works in gamedev as an artist, and got positive feedback. I know it’s not much, but that + my almost 20 years of gamedev experience should be enough for the game to not be a complete garbage. But I am not sure if I would be able to reach the target audience either.
So, the question are – is it worth to risk and go semi-commercial? I even created a bit of funny extra content for the pirate version of the game. But still cannot decide if I should go for it. And if i do - where do i make a post about game that's available for the price and for free at the same time - in commercial or in regular section?

posts.body:
Just a word of advice: I'd be very careful.
There's a lot of predatory pseudo-publishers out there who will take 50% of your earnings for
very little
in the way of actual return. I'm not saying that there's not a ton of great indie publishers out there (in fact, I am very pro-publisher, in general) but I'd be very careful about who you do business with.
Generally, if people are being obtuse, or promising the stars, it's generally a good idea to ask to see their publishing portfolio to see if there's anything on there that you actually recognise.
If not, it's usually just someone looking to make money off your labour for very little investment. Don't forget, if the $100 upload fee is a lot, you can host the game on other storefronts first to drum up that capital without having to engage with someone who is going to do nothing for you except front you $100 for an ROI many, many times higher than that. Especially if that 50% is "profit share", which means that you also foot the 30% steam fee.
If you do look to engage with a publisher: Find out what they'll do for your project - do they have skills or resources to help with development? Do they offer QA, or marketing? Do they have existing relationships that you can leverage, such as Steam contacts (or even storefront takeovers).
Don't forget: Finding indies from areas where $100 is a difficult sum to scrape together is a great deal for the publisher, but not such a great deal for the aspiring indie.

posts.author: SawyerFriend
posts.body:
I think Brew's idea of using other platforms like Itch to build up money to get past the Steam paywall is a great idea! I also want to point out that if your game is good enough, you can definitely sell to publishers that don't necessarily deal in RPG Maker games exclusively (in fact, I highly recommend you seek one of those publishers out, if you take that road). Remember that there have been a lot of extremely successful indie RPGs in the last five years, and many publishers are eager to hop on a quality product if it looks like it could see a fraction of Omori or Sea of Stars' numbers.
Furthermore, this is a sentiment I hear repeated constantly in the industry and one I would like to echo again: you should be the one reaching out to publishers. I would advise against taking a deal with someone who you did not actively pitch your game to, because it's often a sign that they aren't frequently having games pitched to them. My recommendation is to look at games that have publishers that are similar to yours, keep a big list of them, and start reaching out to them with a well made pitch deck. There are lots of resources online that can help you find a good way to pitch your game, and you could even make a thread to get feedback in here!
Just remember that a publisher isn't a magic button that triples your sales: a publisher can only provide value if they're good at what they do.
Now, moving away from the publisher talk for a sec and examining the greater look at monetized games, this is something I have a lot of experience with myself, as I was not interested in monetizing my own work for a very long time. There are a few pros and cons you might have missed, which I'd like to lay out here if you don't mind!
Pro:
-Algorithms on all platforms favour revenue above all else. If your game is free, it cannot make money and will always be penalized by the algorithm.
-A monetized game exudes confidence that you've got a quality product and tells the world "I made a thing worth paying for!" It can often look better than a free game.
Con:
-A paid game can become less accessible. Like you said, $100 is a lot of money for some people, so even a $10 price tag could be someone's food budget that week. Furthermore, any amount of money on a digital storefront bars access to anyone who cannot pay for something digitally (e.g. children without credit cards)
-A paid game leads to additional expenses. If anyone else is working on your game, you will need to sit down and discuss compensation with them. You'll very likely need to pay some sort of income tax, possibly set up an LLC or small business, it can be a lot of paperwork.
-You aren't guaranteed to make much, if any, money back. Just like was mentioned above, many games simply don't make any money at all, and this would not negate the other cons here. I want to make especially clear that if your life is depending on the additional income, like you eluded to in the original post, I would advise heavily against gambling it on your game. There is money to be made from RPG Maker games, but the statistics are weighed heavily against us. I highly recommend treating this as a hobby first, especially if you did not originally begin this venture with monetization in mind.
So! TL;DR a publisher is a good idea, but do your research and reach out to publishers yourself rather than letting them come to you. Remember that there is no guaranteed income here and that it is ill advised to spend money you can't afford to lose on this venture.
At the end of the day, monetization is a great way to help your game get seen by more eyes, and I think you can make a bit of money off of it too, but temper your expectations!

is a great place to start learning!)

It's worth noting that Steam's revenue split is worthwhile just because, whether this is a good thing or not, Steam controls the PC gaming market at the moment. They're a storefront, similar to selling a product at Wal-Mart; the ability to have your product on the shelves of that store at all inspires confidence in the consumer, and more importantly, it's in a location that consumers are already visiting.
Steam isn't a publisher, it's a store, which is providing a very different service that is important to distinguish for people that are new to this side of game development.
I don't know where the 50% number that's been thrown around is coming from, but what I'm starting to gather based on this conversation is that Aldorlea appears to be offering a similar service to Steam; it's a storefront, not a publisher. With that understanding, 50% is still very steep but does more closely resemble a revenue split I would expect from a storefront. What worries me is that it's being referred to as "publishing" (Steam does not publish games, they merely distribute).
There is also a double edged sword to the additional visibility of new releases, which is that it creates a lot of sludge that needs to be navigated in order to find quality products. This is why Steam puts so much emphasis on only giving screen real estate to games that are already popular; they want to ensure that the first thing the end user sees when they open the store is quality games that they might actually want to buy.
